implementation_notes: Node ships no ORM, and node-postgres is deliberately low level - its docs state that it provides no higher-level abstraction around transactions, so you issue BEGIN/COMMIT yourself on a single checked-out client. The cluster lock is therefore the SQL lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the aggregate root row inside the transaction, after which every member write is covered until COMMIT, with an optional version column when you prefer optimistic checking. The pool replaces a lock manager for connection handling, not for locking: the lock lives in the database and dies with the transaction. Sequelize users express the same thing with transaction + lock options instead of hand-written SQL.
idiom_name: pg transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on the root row (node-postgres)
pitfalls: A transaction must use one client: issuing BEGIN through pool.query gives the statements to different connections, so the lock is taken on a connection that does not own the rest of the work.
The single-threaded event loop does not remove the need for the lock - requests interleave at every await, so two handlers can load the same cluster before either commits.
Always release the client in a finally block and roll back on error; a leaked client with an open transaction keeps the root locked and starves the pool.
